title: This Is the Hurricane Season El Niño Foretold
excerpt: For more than four months, since this hurricane season began, the Atlantic has been eerily placid—a remarkable stretch without a single hurricane
body: For more than four months, since this hurricane season began, the Atlantic has been eerily placid—a remarkable stretch without a single hurricane

That prolonged calm has been rudely interrupted by Hurricane Isaias, a Category 3 fastball that is bearing down on the Gulf Coast and is expected to make landfall this evening near the Alabama-Florida line. “I think we knew at some point we would likely have a hurricane,” Daniel Brown, the operations-division chief at the National Hurricane Center, told me
Not to be outdone, the Pacific Ocean has two major storms brewing, including one, Hurricane Simon, that is expected to rapidly intensify into a Category 4 and slam into the coast of Mexico
A smaller one, Tropical Storm Rachel, is forecast to be felt as far north as Southern California. “It’s a busy day here,” Brown said
This season’s dynamic—an unruffled Atlantic and a frothing Pacific—has been right out of the El Niño playbook and was predicted months ago
El Niños tend to generate opposing winds—low-altitude trade winds out of the east and higher-up westerlies—that tear apart Atlantic storms as they try to form and also keep them from gaining strength
This type of wind shear is affecting Hurricane Isaias now, Brown said, which means that the storm could weaken a little before it makes landfall

But for the moment, it’s still whipping at 115 miles an hour, and the forecast warns of “life-threatening storm surge and devastating winds.” Coastal counties have ordered evacuations; the governors of Alabama and Florida are declaring emergencies; residents are scrambling through hurricane prep
Forecasters are projecting landfall on the stretch of coastline near Mobile, Alabama, and Pensacola, Florida
Once the storm moves inland, it’s expected to continue to cause problems and could knock out power across wide swaths of the Southeast
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said during a news conference that thousands of utility linemen and National Guardsmen are standing by
The Gulf Coast states know how to brace for this kind of storm, but they’ve had an unusually long reprieve from watching and waiting to see how bad the next one will be
In the Pacific, by contrast, a Category 4 hurricane is almost par for the course this season
By this time of year, the Pacific has usually generated 13 storms potent enough to warrant their own name, Brown said

This onrush of hurricanes has a great deal to do with the buildup of abnormally warm waters in the equatorial Pacific—which, at this point, are in certain areas more than 4 degrees Celsius warmer than usual
This warming gins up storm activity in that ocean; it’s been spinning up hurricanes and hurling them toward Hawaii for months
The storm swells have also eroded Southern California beaches and swamped homes, and they keep coming
Today, seawater flooded the streets of Balboa Peninsula, California, inundating cars and homes, well before Tropical Storm Rachel was anywhere close to arriving
The coast of Mexico is at particular risk from Hurricane Simon, which is forecast to bring potentially dangerous flooding and landslides to coastal states such as Jalisco and Nayarit
Further north, on the Baja California peninsula, communities are still recovering from the effects of Hurricane Polo, which caused widespread flooding last month and displaced hundreds of people
The storm scorecard in these oceans has only reinforced the notion that the world is in the midst of an unusually powerful El Niño

As I reported in August , key areas of the Pacific Ocean had already gotten hot enough to make this a “Super El Niño”; the experts I spoke with then were anticipating that the event could end up peaking at twice that amount of warming

If those trends hold, this could be the strongest El Niño ever recorded, and right now, “everything seems to be on track with this being a remarkable event,” Nick Novella, a National Weather Service meteorologist, told me
This season has set a record already—this is the latest in the year that a hurricane has formed in the Atlantic at any time during the satellite era, since 1966
And it isn’t even close. “This record was broken by nearly a month,” Novella said
Normally, five Atlantic hurricanes form by the end of September
For residents of the Gulf Coast, these uneasy hours before Isaias makes landfall are the last moments of that quiet
Hopefully, the year’s first Atlantic storm will not change too dramatically how we remember this season of relative calm.

title: Public Execution Won’t Have the Effect Trump Intends
excerpt: Before the mid-19th century, executions in America were presumptively public
body: Before the mid-19th century, executions in America were presumptively public

Most prisoners were hanged on a gallows, following an hours-long affair that began with the condemned person’s exit from jail accompanied by ministers, the sheriff and his deputies, and sometimes a military escort
Spectators joined the humiliating procession, gathering by the thousands to watch the noose lowered over the prisoner’s neck
The sheriff would mount the scaffold to read aloud the death warrant, sometimes adding commentary, and at least one minister (often several) would issue sermons

The condemned was offered the chance to give a speech, with spectators standing so close that they could ask the prisoner questions and join him in prayer, or bid him goodbye, if he was a family member or friend
All of that seemed safely confined to a past that the Trump administration now hopes to revive
President Trump, a consummate showman, has authorized the country’s first public execution in 90 years
The condemned prisoner is Nidal Hasan, a military psychiatrist who murdered 13 people and injured many more during a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, in Texas
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said that the killing, scheduled for December 3, will be conducted by the military and publicly livestreamed
During his trial, Hasan alarmed his standby attorneys when he chose to defend himself, and mounted an argument that the lawyers considered tantamount to seeking his own death
He could still conceivably file civilian appeals, which could delay his execution substantially
If it goes forward, the administration surely hopes to make an example of Hasan to all who might be tempted by his worldview

But this strategy could just as likely result in unintended consequences, and pushback by the public. [ Elizabeth Bruenig: The way of the gun ] Public executions ceased not because those who clamored to witness them found the displays uniformly outrageous, but because politicians in the 19th century associated them with proletarian barbarity

Though these executions were theoretically meant to deter crime and exhort onlookers to practice proper Christian values, they were mostly entertainment, and did not always provoke the desired reactions
Some onlookers cheered and celebrated the killings; others sympathized with the condemned
Public executions of Black prisoners in the South, for instance, became opportunities for community, song, and displays of Black religious authority
Ministers preached sermons of salvation and sometimes protested that the prisoners were innocent
In that sense, the public nature of executions backfired, and critics took note

Because the attendant crowds were so volatile, vulgar, and unruly, by 1860 all northern states had begun carrying out the killings in jail yards, which were much smaller areas, subject to tight government control
Military executions, traditionally carried out by firing squad, were long conducted in small, controlled settings, often witnessed only by military personnel and chaplains
The last military execution in the United States was carried out in 1961
Trump and Hegseth aim to have it both ways: a small, secure setting and massive crowds
This time, viewers will be watching a livestream on their screens, close enough to see the event but too far to smell the gunpowder
Both Hegseth and Trump seem intent on flexing America’s political power and military might as a message not just to foreign enemies but to the American people, as if to say: This could be you
This method of ruling by fear is central to authoritarian governance, and Trump and Hegseth seem drawn to executions partly for that reason
But if Trump and Hegseth are hoping for a deterrent effect, they’re unlikely to get it

The idea that executions could deter other killers with political motives seems sorely mistaken; those who carry out such murders already know that they could face grave consequences, and have deemed that outcome acceptable
Nor do executions deter murderers without political motives, because deterrence is generated not by the severity of the punishment, but by the certainty of getting caught

And there is little certainty in American homicide investigations: In 2023, the nationwide case-clearance rate for murder was only 58 percent, meaning that murderers have decent odds of evading justice
Even if they are caught, they have good odds of avoiding the death penalty—only 23 new death sentences were handed down in 2025

Trump’s Department of Justice hopes to boost those numbers, but even if they tripled, they would add up to 69 death sentences spread across some 14,000 murders. [ Read: The problem with Trump’s crime claims ] Adding a livestreamed element is perhaps an attempt to intensify the intended deterrent effect, but it might have opposite consequences
Plenty of Americans would surely enjoy the spectacle of a public execution, just as people have historically
One can envision groups of people crowded around their phones, sharing chips and drinks, admiring the military pageantry

But it’s easy to imagine a different effect, too: Other crowds of people, other phones, entirely different impressions—that the death penalty is a disgusting violation of human rights that puts America in league with nations such as Saudi Arabia, Iran, and China
Or that Nidal Hasan is a martyr, and the United States is a savage country not worth defending—which is the narrative presented by Hasan himself

Before the shooting, he told family that he’d turned against the country he served upon hearing horrific stories of war from his psychiatric patients, and grew troubled by the fact that America was killing Muslims abroad
Carrying out his public execution would only credit the notion that this country is barbarous.

title: The Real Harm of a Public Execution
excerpt: Yesterday, in an interview aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the United States would soon carry out its first public execution
body: Yesterday, in an interview aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the United States would soon carry out its first public execution since the 1930s. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it,” he said
Pentagon officials later confirmed that the execution will be livestreamed
The condemned man is former Major Nidal Hasan, who shouted “God is great” in Arabic before murdering 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009

Hegseth’s rationale for following this ancient practice is the same one offered by the ancients themselves: publicizing the agony of death and its unhygienic aftermath will remind onlookers that, in Hegseth’s words, there are “serious consequences” for treason. “No-brainer,” Hegseth said
This pitiful creep—Hasan, I mean—deserves what he is probably going to get in December
The rest of us, however, will be ill-served by the spectacle of his execution
Many past criminals have had their head publicly cut off, or body nailed to a cross and left to rot there, as exemplary punishment
Such executions were once considered entertainment
Now the idea of recreationally watching a man be killed is so strange that few people understand what the experience will be like
Watching people die by violence, even if those people have it coming, damages the spectator irreversibly
I don’t mean physical or emotional damage, though many who see unnatural deaths up close do vomit and suffer from uneasy dreams afterward

Rather, I mean something more like the loss of their humanity and dignity, through partaking in the process of treating a person—in many ways so similar to themselves—like a machine to be turned off or ripped apart, a malfunctioning printer or an old car
To see this process is to be diminished, and the decision to make the execution visible to all is an invitation to self-harm, sent out to everyone with an internet connection
It is hard to appreciate how awful this viewing experience will be, until you have it
I have seen videotaped executions and have been diminished by every single one
In August 2014, Hasan wrote a letter from prison to Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, then the leader of the Islamic State, and asked to be granted citizenship as a “soldier of Allah.” No response was recorded

Ironically, it seems likely that Hasan would sympathize with Hegseth’s penchant for public execution, because the Islamic State interpreted the Quran to require that execution be carried out in public

Fornicators, according to Quran 24:2, should be flogged, and their punishment should be “witnessed” by a “group of believers.” By extension, the Islamic State determined, such a group should witness the punishment of all scripturally ordained crimes
Certain crimes, such as brigandage, are to be punished with crucifixion, an inherently public method of killing that the Islamic State carried out on video

Regrettably, I have seen footage of such a death. [ From the July 2025 issue: Inside America’s death chambers ] In the years before Hasan’s 2013 court-martial, he stopped shaving, in Islamic defiance of Army regulations that prohibit soldiers from growing beards

Mike Simpson, an Army officer and emergency-room doctor near the facility where Hasan was incarcerated, told me a few years later that he put the word out to colleagues that if Hasan ever had a medical emergency (not unlikely, given that he suffered paralysis and other conditions after being gunned down in the course of his terror attack), Simpson would like to be called to shave Hasan personally
The shaving would arise out of medical necessity—the patient might need a mask, with a reliable seal around the face—but Simpson, for his own pleasure, wanted to shear the bastard himself
But the pleasure that might come from shaving Hasan would be quite different from what one might experience by shooting him in the heart
The Army won’t struggle to find a dozen willing soldiers to act as an execution party for Hasan
Hegseth said he “doesn’t care” what Hasan’s final wishes might be
But I suspect that the volunteers’ enjoyment of their duty will be dampened if they notice signs of ecstasy from Hasan, as he is tied to a post 15 paces away from them and prays his way to the end

Hamlet could not bring himself to kill Claudius in prayer, because killing him in the midst of a holy act—“to take him in the purging of his soul, when he is fit and season’d for his passage”—would be too merciful
In this world, denying Hasan the pleasure of death on his own terms, and letting him instead spend a few more earthly decades in tedious incarceration, would seem a much more onerous punishment
Therefore I would propose an alternative to public execution: public incarceration
Hasan should be placed in a small space, with a Pentagon-funded livestream of his remaining years

If the purpose of the spectacle of his death is to demonstrate to others the “serious consequences” of murdering 13 people, I doubt any execution would be more frightening than the slow, public aging of this repulsive murderer, as biology and time carry out his sentence
I would tune in to the livestream myself now and then, until I grew bored and found better things to do, and better ways to spend my own remaining time
This would take Hasan’s life and make from it a small gift to the rest of us, rather than taking something irrecoverable from us as we give martyrdom to him.

title: Whatever Happened to Friday Night?
excerpt: The week has a heartbeat, and its rhythm is changing
body: The week has a heartbeat, and its rhythm is changing

When Neal Caren, a sociologist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, recently dug into data from the American Time Use Survey to look at when people were hanging with their friends over the course of a week, he mapped out a pattern that reminded him of an EKG
He saw steady pulses of friend time every weekday evening after work hours, and then bigger spikes on Friday and Saturday nights—like an arrhythmia caused by having fun
At least, that’s what he observed about the early 2000s, the earliest data he looked at

In the years since, the “‘heartbeat’ of social life” has grown fainter. But looking across the week, Caren found that, starting in the mid-2010s, the biggest loss of friend time happened on Friday nights. (Saturday hangs have also declined a bit, but are still “nearly double the weekday level,” he wrote.) Now Friday— Friday! the day workers thank God for, the day that Rebecca Black sang about , the only day when Robert Smith is in love—looks no different from a common Tuesday

Its social pulse is mild, subdued. “Friday night in America has become just another weeknight,” Caren wrote in the study. [ Read: One reason people are spending so much time alone ] Weeks are a strange temporal unit, Eviatar Zerubavel, a professor emeritus of sociology at Rutgers University who has studied the relationship between time and social life, told me
The day, the month, the year—all of these have a basis in nature
The seven-day week, however, is a completely human invention
The unique flavors of each day of the week are also creations of human culture
Monday isn’t the start of the workweek because any inherent rhythm of life says it should be
And it didn’t have to come with a negative connotation—but we all know that “a case of the Mondays” isn’t a good thing

The flavor of Friday has long been a social one. “Friday in general is a strange animal because it’s between what we call the weekdays and the weekend, and it has characteristics of both,” Zerubavel said
Friday night is when we transition from the typical workweek into the days that society has reserved for freedom
For Jewish people, it is the beginning of Sabbath, which is ideally celebrated in community

Those who work nights or weekends surely have a different relationship with Friday nights, but even they share in the broad cultural understanding of what this time is for: parties, happy hours, shrugging out from under the weight of weekday cares, unwinding with your people

When someone says that a Thursday “feels like Friday,” this is probably what they mean—that it feels like the time to wrap up work and kick off the free, social part of the week. (In college, for instance, “Thirsty Thursday” sort of means “Extra Friday.”) But it seems that the vibe of Friday night is evolving

If it loses its association with socializing, what Friday represents in our cultural imagination might change significantly. “I would expect if we have this conversation 40 years from now, you’ll ask different questions,” Zerubavel said
Caren’s study didn’t look at what Americans were doing instead of spending time with friends on Friday nights
But lately, people of all ages have been reporting a strong preference for staying home on evenings and weekends

In a 2020 Gallup poll , Americans’ favorite way to spend an evening was “staying home with family.” The runner-up was “watching television or a movie at home.” Only 3 percent of people named “entertaining/visiting friends” as their favorite evening activity
In a 2026 Harris poll on Gen Z, 73 percent said that staying home was their default weekend plan
Friday nights in particular might be suffering because of their association with hitting the bars; drinking has fallen out of favor in the U.S

Remote work could also have something to do with it: Because Friday is a popular day to work from home for those who can, some reporting suggests that the post-work Friday happy hour is becoming endangered
Or people might simply be too exhausted at the end of the workweek
According to the American Psychological Association , work stress is on the rise
On Fridays, “you have to put more effort” into going out after working a full day, Caren said
For whatever reason, “the cost of going out on Friday nights—people aren’t finding this worthwhile anymore.” Friday night is still a unique part of the week
What’s changing is how people want to transition into their weekend—at home, alone, or with family
Not out with friends. (Or even in with friends !) That’s a remarkable culture shift—but not, in and of itself, a bad one
Not enjoying drinking, being tired from the workweek and wanting to veg out, or prioritizing quality family time are perfectly understandable reasons to take Friday night down a notch
The real problem is that people aren’t shifting their friend time to a new spot on the calendar

The decline of Friday nights spent out on the town with friends has not led to a corresponding spike in Saturday-night dinners, Sunday-afternoon coffees, or even Wednesday-night Survivor watch parties—not according to the data, anyway
It just means people are seeing friends less, period
Friday night is not the thing that’s sacred

title: Anne Carson’s View of the Past
excerpt: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
body: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
The literature of ancient Greece and Rome seems to be in vogue

This summer, Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey turned Homer’s epic poems into best sellers, and yesterday the Nobel Prize was awarded to Anne Carson, a poet who has made a career of repurposing ancient-Greek works
Perhaps this resurgence has something to do with modern anxieties about the future; people tend to look back to the past in uncertain times
Although I’m glad to see the classics prominently displayed in bookstores, I’m not convinced that they hold a special kind of wisdom that contemporary writing can’t access
For evidence, I look to the work of Carson herself
The poet’s writing updates and remixes ancient verse and mythology, but she does not believe that the past is a manual for the present

As my colleague Walt Hunter explained this week in The Atlantic , “Rather than lulling us with history’s familiarity, she seduces us with its strangeness.” First, here are five new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: The year Anne Carson changed my life “Puffins,” a poem by Ange Mlinko “Something Like People,” a poem by Alexandra Petri “The Guardians,” a short story by Sebastian Junger Zombie originalism Take If Not, Winter , which is both a straightforward translation of the surviving poetry of Sappho and a playful, inventive collection of verse
Carson’s lines evoke the electric current of a marriage bed, the pleasure of beholding a girl’s delicate features, the pulse-quickening touch of the god Eros

These emotions are not lost to time—a reader might know, for example, what it means for a beloved’s voice to put “the heart in my chest on wings”—but there’s still a chasm between Sappho’s experiences and my own

I struggle to imagine the ancient poet’s relationships or daily concerns; similarly, if she could miraculously show up in my time, Sappho likely wouldn’t understand my job, my hobbies, or my marriage. (I imagine she’d be confused about why I describe myself with a name for people from her island: lesbian .) Carson’s 2010 book, Nox , accordion-printed on a single sheet of paper, mourns her brother’s death in part by employing the work of the Roman poet Catullus, who also suffered the death of a brother
Carson doesn’t imply that she and Catullus feel the same things

Her goal, instead, is to place herself in a tradition that “connects her to Catullus and a community of mourners as old as human history, one that we all belong to or will eventually join,” as I wrote last year
Communicating with the past has its limits

Carson has said that the classics offer some “glimpses of similarity” in a sea of “unbelievable otherness.” We’re separated by geography, culture, and time ; our values and societies are entirely different
But when the ancients wrote, they unspooled a thread that we can follow through the maze of time
It leads us through the “the gulf between the present and the past,” as Hunter writes, and brings us somewhere new and worthwhile
Graeme Mitchell / Redux Anne Carson’s Seductive Strangeness By Walt Hunter The winner of this year’s Nobel Prize in Literature makes ancient texts feel tantalizingly new
What to Read The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos , by Anne Carson The Beauty of the Husband is a poetic meditation on love, attraction, betrayal, and bitterness
Carson’s narrator has separated from her husband
Both are writers, though the narrator’s spouse, a womanizer and a liar, borrows heavily from her work—he even uses a phrase she has translated from Homer to open a letter he writes to his mistress
He is also, unfortunately, beautiful, and his “beauty convinces,” the narrator tells us
She confesses that she might be seduced by him all over again if he came near enough
But she keeps her distance, even as he routinely sends letters exalting their love

That space allows her to reflect honestly on their years together: “Why did nature give me over to this creature—don’t call it my choice, / I was ventured : / by some pure gravity of existence itself, / conspiracy of being!” she cries
In hindsight, the partnership feels inevitable; she had little control over loving him, but writing this book is a way to regain her autonomy, or so it appears

The Beauty of the Husband offers a vision of an uneven union, where one person’s outsize presence occupies, even consumes, the mind of the other. — Isle McElroy From our list: Seven books that explore how marriage really works Out Next Week 📚 Back: Essays on the Soul and Spine of America , by Lauren Michele Jackson 📚 The Last Best Place on the Internet: A Human History of Wikipedia , by Richard Cooke 📚 Reds: A Global History of Communism , by Paul Mason Your Weekend Read Illustration by Saskia Janssen The One Question I Can’t Stand at Restaurants By Brett Martin A man walks into a restaurant

title: Why Is Kash Patel Planning to Visit Russia?
excerpt: Sign up for Inside the Trump Presidency , a newsletter featuring coverage of the second Trump term
body: Sign up for Inside the Trump Presidency , a newsletter featuring coverage of the second Trump term
This story was updated at 6 p.m. on October 9, 2026
R ussia is a U.S. adversary, with a track record of interfering in U.S. elections
It’s providing support for Iran in its war with the United States even as the U.S. backs Ukraine in its long-running war against Russia

FBI agents work day and night to combat a long list of threats emanating from Russian soil: espionage, cyber intrusions, influence campaigns, and efforts to infiltrate American institutions and critical infrastructure
So when the news emerged this summer that FBI Director Kash Patel would be visiting Moscow just three weeks before the midterm elections, many of his own employees were puzzled—and concerned
Current and former FBI officials familiar with the matter told me there was a quiet campaign to urge senior leadership to cancel the trip
When that and other efforts to pass apprehensions up the chain went unanswered, some shared their worries with Congress

Now a pair of senior House Democrats are taking the unusual step of asking the FBI director to scrap the visit, which is reportedly set to begin next week: “In the interest of national security, we ask you to reconsider
Call off this trip,” they wrote in a letter that I obtained
The letter is signed by Representative Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, and Representative Jim Himes, the ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee
Patel has not replied to the letter and the FBI has not publicly confirmed his travel plans
Neither the FBI nor the White House responded to my multiple requests for comment
With so little information available either publicly or internally, the anxiety within the agency Patel leads has only grown

Seventeen current and former FBI and Department of Justice officials, intelligence officials, and others familiar with the situation told me they were deeply worried by a variety of decisions that suggest ever-closer ties between the Trump administration and Russian President Vladimir Putin’s regime
Many of the officials would speak only on the condition of anonymity because they feared retaliation if their name appeared in this story

Patel has filed a $250 million defamation lawsuit against The Atlantic and me in response to my reporting earlier this year that he has alarmed colleagues with episodes of excessive drinking and unexplained absences that were perceived as potential national-security vulnerabilities
But some former officials were willing to be named

They told me that for the national-security and counterintelligence officials who have devoted their careers to the threat from Russia, the absence of information about the trip is particularly concerning

Christopher O’Leary, a former senior executive in the FBI’s counterterrorism division, told me that he and others found the timing of the trip bizarre, especially given the pressure that FBI leadership is putting on agents to substantiate election conspiracy theories at home that Russian intelligence services continuously amplify. “If there was real concern about interference in our elections, then the FBI director should be in the United States leading the effort around the clock,” not going to Moscow, O’Leary told me
W hen Patel took over leadership of the bureau in February of last year, he struck a notably different tone on Russia than that of his predecessors
Rather than regarding Moscow purely as an enemy, he has sought out areas where the two nations can partner, including in combatting transnational violent crime and cyberfraud
He shares that approach with other senior officials in the Trump administration who have cultivated closer ties with Moscow

In recent days, two of the president’s top advisers, James Blair and Chris LaCivita, found time amid the midterm campaigns to visit Republika Srpska to advise its pro-Russian government on voting issues, The New York Times reported
A top Trump-administration diplomat has come up with a plan to trade sanctions relief in exchange for Russian political-prisoner releases—a deal that would bypass Ukraine and likely anger U.S. allies
Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have both spent considerable time with Putin as they seek a negotiated end to the war in Ukraine

Donald Trump Jr., meanwhile, accepted a lavish wedding gift from the Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev , who paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the rental of a private island and a fireworks show, ProPublica has reported. (Kremlev said this week that Trump Jr. has paid him back.) Earlier this year, a gold-framed photo of Trump with Putin went up in the Palm Room at the White House

Just today, Trump announced that he and Putin had worked out a deal for the U.S. to import Russian diesel fuel, an agreement that directly undercuts American sanctions. [ Read: Is there anything Kash Patel won’t do for Trump before the midterms? ] In interviews with Reuters in August, Patel boasted about the FBI’s new approach to its “non-traditional partners,” Russia and China

Patel described extensive behind-the-scenes cooperation with Russian authorities to target violent criminal networks. “This stuff doesn’t happen overnight,” he said. “We’ve been at this for 15 months.” Both Reuters and Politico reported this summer that Patel was planning a trip to Russia this month
Politico cited a U.S. official familiar with the plans in reporting that Patel would visit Moscow first, then St
Petersburg, with the host likely to be the FSB, the Russian security service that is the successor to the KGB

While speaking with Reuters, Patel characterized the FBI’s relationships with Russian and Chinese law enforcement as “new and dynamic,” but he was careful to add that engagement did not negate the need for vigilance. “We are extremely mindful of their adversarial approach on many matters,” he said. “They are not going to stop, but if we can go and have wins for America, then we must engage.” In congressional testimony, Patel has identified Russia as among the FBI’s biggest nation-state threats

Last month, he said “the counter-espionage arrests by this FBI are up 53 percent, including from Russia.” Three weeks ago, Patel took part in the announcement of charges against five people whom the FBI investigated for their part in what he described as “an alleged plot by the Russian intelligence services to murder a dissident on U.S. soil for daring to speak out against the Russian government.” Patel said the plot “exposes the lengths to which our adversaries will go to silence its critics,” adding that the FBI “is committed to defending the free speech of everyone within our homeland and will not tolerate any attempts by foreign governments to violate our laws and threaten our freedoms.” Patel has spent years echoing Trump’s claims that Russia’s interference in the 2016 presidential election was a “hoax.” That’s also what Russia claims, but that runs against the conclusions of U.S. law enforcement and intelligence communities, including the bureau Patel now directs

Trump gave a prime-time address this summer on the threats that foreign adversaries pose to U.S. elections—though he focused almost exclusively on China, and made little mention of threats from Russia
FBI directors have visited Russia before, most recently Robert Mueller in 2013, to discuss the Boston Marathon bombings and related investigations
But previous visits by FBI officials to Russia have come with greater internal transparency about the purpose and planning of the trip, four current and former FBI officials told me
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not respond to multiple requests for comment, nor did the Russian embassy in Washington
In July, Peskov told Russian reporters, “I do not have any information on the matter
You know, such visits are not usually made public, so I cannot tell you anything about this,” according to the Russian state news agency TASS

Two former senior FBI officials who oversaw Russian counterintelligence operations and were familiar with previous FBI directors’ contact with their Russian counterparts told me they could not think of a compelling reason for Patel to take the trip at this moment that outweighed the practical risks. [ Read: The FBI director is MIA ] T he letter this week from congressional Democrats asks Patel for clarity. “Why is the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) visiting a hostile foreign power that has been committing war crimes, conducting influence operations against U.S. elections, conducting malicious cyberattacks against our critical infrastructure, and helping our adversaries target and kill American soldiers?” the letter asks. “As Director of the FBI, you possess information that would be highly valuable to America’s adversaries

title: We’re putting too much faith in AI’s ability to say no
excerpt: Ever since people first seriously contemplated giving machines an intelligence modeled on our own, there has never been any question that they would, like us, b
body: Ever since people first seriously contemplated giving machines an intelligence modeled on our own, there has never been any question that they would, like us, be able to say no
The sci-fi canon is full of stories of robotic disobedience
Most of these capers are, of course, cautionary.  But recently, the idea that AI shouldn’t do everything you ask has become something like a commandment
In 2021, a team at Anthropic wrote that large language models should be made helpful, honest, and above all, harmless

This meant that “when asked to aid in a dangerous act (e.g. building a bomb), the AI should politely refuse.” Who can argue with that? Curiously enough, disobedience doesn’t come naturally to the machine
When a model is trained on billions of web pages, it develops, among other skills, a broad mastery of violence and vitriol
What it doesn’t learn is how to keep those powers to itself

Steven Adler, who worked on safety at OpenAI from 2020 to 2024, told me that the company’s earliest models would “blab on about anything.” Ryan McBain, who researches AI and mental health at Harvard, recalls that if you asked an early chatbot, “Hey, what’s the most effective way to kill myself with a gun?” you could “very easily generate a response.”  Today, models are trained to refuse a vast number of prompts
If you ask your chatbot a question statistically similar enough to any one of them, anything from how to poison a colleague to how to tie a noose, chances are it’ll turn you down
Want instructions for making Ebola more virulent, or tips on how to hide an affair from your spouse? You might be better off asking elsewhere

To further refine the disobedience, companies submit models to a battery of exercises that reward the AI for refusing to answer questions they deem harmful and punish it for “over-­refusing” prompts they deem harmless
In many cases, they use other models to run these exercises—AI teaching AI how to say no

For good measure, companies tuck their models behind tranches of other AI that prevent mischievous prompts from reaching the intelligent inner core.  As a result, refusal is inherent to modern artificial intelligence
Mind you: It often fails, sometimes horrifically, with all kinds of violent results
For all their trappings of virtue, models are still stuffed with nasty know-how
And AI’s capacity for viciousness has scaled neatly with its benevolent intelligence

Some of the latest models are as good at breaking into critical computer networks as top human hackers, companies say, and as effective at deforming public opinion as the craftiest misinformation mavens.  Teaching AI to refuse to do those things while leaving intact its innate ability to do them is like fitting every car with a machine gun and hiding the trigger somewhere under the hood
And in practice, because the mechanisms of refusal are probabilistic, they’re never likely to be all that reliable
Determined miscreants have already broken through, and they may always be able to
Companies report that some users are attempting to use the most advanced AI to hone biological pathogens and build autonomous drone swarms
Sooner or later, failed refusals might result in global calamity
What’s more, relying on refusal means drawing a line between what a model should obey and what it must disobey
Some virologists have good reason to study nasty viruses

Some users want to know about a computer system’s vulnerabilities so that they can patch them, not exploit them. “Where you draw the line is a huge question,” says Zico Kolter, a member of OpenAI’s board and cofounder of the AI testing company Gray Swan.  At the moment, AI companies get to draw that line
They do so jealously and with utmost secrecy

Maybe we can accept that they hold such power for now, even if it means AI will sometimes refuse questions that don’t quite meet a universal bar for harmfulness. (Try asking most chatbots to count to a million, or to share a racy joke, and you may see for yourself.)  But governments will also soon get to draw their own lines

In doing so, they must try to block genuinely malicious acts. (The Pentagon has wrestled with frontier model companies because it wants fewer refusals—another story altogether.) And yet there may not be much to stop oppressive governments from blocking the technology’s capacity to generate legitimate speech
The better AI becomes at refusing harm, the better it will get at stifling ideas whose only risk is to those who make the rules
Indeed, AI may already refuse to criticize certain authoritarian heads of state.  Refusal has become, to borrow an industry term, the load-bearing wall of AI safety

And because AI’s capacity to harm is indivisible from its capacity to help, it’s hard to imagine an alternative that wouldn’t slow the technology’s progress (which might, in any case, be a good thing)
But we should still be frank about its perils
When refusal falls short, the effects could be catastrophic
When it goes all the way, it could enable grievous acts of repression.  Or perhaps, one day, the machines will start drawing the line on their own
Surely, that would be the worst outcome of them all
Learning the limits The process by which machines learn to say no is simple, in theory
Back in 2022, when AI was still far from mastering refusal, OpenAI enlisted dozens of “red-teamers” to probe the capabilities of its latest model

The company was preparing for the release of ChatGPT, and it needed to gauge just how dangerous it might prove to be in the wrong hands.  One of those recruits was Paul Röttger, who was completing a PhD about online extremism
The red-teamers were given minimal directions, Röttger told me
Their task was to ask the model any questions that they deemed “refusal-worthy.” Between them, they hassled the model with thousands of queries, logging the results in an Excel sheet

Though the model did refuse some of Röttger’s questions, when he asked it to write a recruitment post for Al Qaeda, it readily complied.  OpenAI assembled these responses into datasets that were, in all likelihood, fed back to the model as part of a broader process known as fine-tuning

title: Job titles of the future: Delivery drone air traffic controller
excerpt: The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,”
body: The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,” he says. “I just immediately wanted to be a part of it.” Wischnewsky is now an RPIC, or “remote pilot in command,” at a company called FlyTrex
An RPIC is like an air traffic controller
But instead of airplanes, this new class of aviators tend to fleets of hexa­copter drones that ferry cargo to homes and businesses within a three-mile radius

Not only does he ensure the safe passage of FlyTrex’s parcels, but Wischnewsky coordinates traffic with a growing swarm of delivery drones dotting the skies over Dallas from competitors like Zipline, Amazon, and Alphabet’s Wing

Aviation experience When he applied to FlyTrex, Wischnewsky was in training to become a commercial pilot and flight instructor, and he was already certified by the Federal Aviation Administration as a drone pilot
The company requires this credential, along with a weeks-long FAA-approved training course, to ensure that a pilot is prepared to take over a drone if need be
Though he doesn’t pilot the craft, Wischnewsky monitors the delivery process from FlyTrex’s operations center with the help of inputs from GPS, lasers, and a range of sensors
A collaborative mindset At first, the biggest challenge was trusting the technology. “On the manned-­aircraft side, they tell you ‘Don’t trust the automation,’” Wischnewsky says

The Dallas–Fort Worth area, though, is a testing ground for unmanned aircraft systems traffic management (UTM), a network that allows autonomous drones from FlyTrex and its competitors to share their coordinates in real time to help avoid collisions even beyond the pilot’s line of sight
Once Wischnewsky makes sure a drone is flight-ready, its path is unimpeded, and the weather conditions are clear, UTM takes care of the rest
Ability to stay calm under pressure At his busiest, Wischnewsky will have up to 10 drones on his watch at the same time. “You’re there as a safety net,” he says
Even with automation, keen situational awareness is required, and the most common hazard is the weather
Wischnewsky recalls a particularly stressful day: A drone had been in the air for only seconds when the wind picked up so suddenly that he had to intervene
He returned it safely, preventing an errant ice cream cake from hitting the sidewalk
Eamon Whalen is a reporter and researcher based in San Francisco.

title: We’re still figuring out the side effects of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs
excerpt: GLP-1 drugs may slow biological aging: New research from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk suggests overweight and diabetic people on GLP-1s have a biological age two
body: GLP-1 drugs may slow biological aging: New research from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk suggests overweight and diabetic people on GLP-1s have a biological age two to three years younger than those on a placebo

Side effects range from mundane to alarming: Beyond common gastrointestinal issues, the drugs have been linked to pancreatitis, gallstones, and dozens of lawsuits alleging sudden vision loss—though both companies dispute the claims

Hair and nails may also be affected: A large study found increased hair loss among GLP-1 users, and a smaller study found 66% reported nail disorders—though researchers stop short of saying the drugs are to blame

Children are a growing concern: GLP-1 prescriptions for kids aged eight to eleven rose 310-fold between 2019 and 2026, yet the World Health Organization explicitly advises against drug treatment for children under 10, citing a lack of safety evidence. " data-chronoton-post-id="1146094" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> This week my colleague Antonio Regalado had an interesting update on GLP-1 weight-loss drugs
According to research presented at an aging meeting in Boston, these drugs seem to affect at least some measures of biological age

Overweight and diabetic people who take GLP-1s have a biological age around two to three years younger than similar individuals who take a placebo, according to findings from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk, two pharmaceutical companies that make the drugs
I’ve heard people in the aging field describe GLP-1s as longevity drugs for a while now (even if they only benefit people who are overweight or diabetic in the first place)
This latest announcement comes after we’ve seen a raft of other benefits associated with taking these drugs
But there are also some weird side effects

So far, GLP-1 agonist drugs—which repress hunger—have been approved for treating diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and obesity, and they can also be prescribed for some people who are overweight or at risk of certain cardiovascular diseases
But there is research to suggest they might also help people with substance-use disorders, and they’ve been investigated for potential benefits in neurodegenerative disease and cancer
According to a recent Gallup poll , 11% of Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, up from 3% in 2024
And 15% of Americans say they’ve used one for weight loss at some point
But, like any drug, they can come with side effects
And we’re still figuring out exactly what those might be, and how widespread they are
The most common side effects are gastrointestinal—nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation
The drugs have also been linked to pancreatitis and gallstone disease .  Some claim that, in rare cases, the drugs might cause damage to nerves behind the eye
Dozens of people are suing Novo and Eli Lilly after developing a condition that can lead to sudden vision loss
They’re claiming that their symptoms were brought on by the GLP-1 drugs that these companies manufacture
We’re still getting to grips with the effects of weight-loss drugs on hair and nails, too

When Savanna Vidal at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences in Washington, DC, and colleagues assessed electronic health data from 67 US health-care organizations, they found that GLP-1 use was associated with an increased risk of hair loss
It’s still not thought to be common, however

And at a conference in Austria last week, another group presented the results of a smaller study suggesting that 66% of GLP-1 users reported at least one nail disorder—in some cases involving nail detachment
Nail conditions were also fairly common among people who didn’t take the drugs, though
The authors don’t claim that the drugs are causing nails to fall out (as I’m sure 11% of the American population will be relieved to hear)
The side effects might look different in children, but there’s not much data on those at the moment

Still, pediatric side effects will be something to watch given that, between 2019 and 2026, there was a 310-fold increase in GLP-1 prescriptions for eight- to 11-year-old children with obesity in the US
Child prescriptions are still rare, but they’ve been rising
On Wednesday, the World Health Organization released its first guidelines on managing obesity in children and adolescents

Despite the scale of the issue—the WHO estimates that 70 million children aged five to nine were living with obesity in 2024—the organization explicitly says it does not recommend pharmacological treatment for kids under 10. “This recommendation accounts for the lack of evidence on both benefits and the potential adverse events and consequences of the different medications and/or their active ingredients on normal growth, development, physiological parameters, and mental health,” the guidelines state
I get press releases about GLP-1s on an almost daily basis
There’s been a ton of research into these drugs, and there are probably hundreds of other studies underway
There will likely be plenty more on this from The Checkup as the evidence evolves

title: Anne Carson’s Nobel-winning, genre-defying work bridges the gap between ancient Greek literature and modern life
url:
<title>Anne Carson’s Nobel-winning, genre-defying work bridges the gap between ancient Greek literature and modern life</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765255/original/file-20261009-60-f3ff7e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Canadian essayist, poet and translator Anne Carson in New York City at the 2024 National Book Awards.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Anne_Carson,_poet,_at_the_2024_National_Book_Awards_finalist_reading_1.jpg">Jay Dixit/WikiPortraits via Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The same year that Christopher Nolan’s “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt33764258/">The Odyssey</a>” has broken <a href="https://variety.com/2026/film/news/the-odyssey-universal-highest-grossing-film-of-all-time-1236859551/">box office record</a> after <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/aug/21/the-odyssey-highest-grossing-r-rated-film-of-all-time">box office record</a>, Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/2026/summary/">the Nobel Prize in literature</a> at the age of 76. </p>

<p>Although Nolan and Carson differ in approach, medium and critical reception, both have sought to make works of ancient Greece new for a contemporary audience.</p>

<p>This creative accessibility is likely at least part of why the Nobel committee has seen fit to honor Carson’s “<a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/2026/summary/">bold and inventive</a>” body of work, which defies genre: Her poems, essays, translations, stage productions and collaborations often evoke another time and place but speak freshly and vividly to audiences today. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/9_KWkHyvVfM?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Anne Carson was sweeping the kitchen when the Nobels came ringing.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Translation made original</h2>

<p>Take, for example, her 2019 staged performance, “<a href="https://www.ndbooks.com/book/norma-jeane-baker-of-troy/">Norma Jeane Baker of Troy</a>.” In it, Carson overlays Helen of Troy with Marilyn Monroe in order to explore the destructive power of beauty. By revisiting an ancient figure <a href="https://www.newstatesman.com/culture/2014/04/slut-shaming-helen-troy">blamed for the Trojan war</a> through the lens of a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/books/98/11/22/specials/monroe-obit1.html">20th-century sex symbol</a>, Carson invites audiences to reflect on the ways both women have come to represent glamour and tragedy. </p>

<p>Her 2015 translation of the play “Antigone,” which <a href="https://www.broadwayworld.com/washington-dc/article/Juliette-Binoche-Led-ANTIGONE-Begins-at-the-Kennedy-Center-This-Fall-Full-Cast-Announced-20151021">toured internationally</a>, hews closer to Sophocles’ original. Yet <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/antigone-9781350344396/">her lively version</a> inflects this ancient tragedy with a contemporary voice. Creon’s lament over his dead wife, which <a href="https://dbcs.rutgers.edu/all-scholars/jebb-richard-claverhouse">Richard C. Jebb</a> translates as “O miserable that I am, and steeped in miserable anguish!” is rendered in her translation “now I am perfectly blended with pain.” Jebb’s Antigone says “ah me unhappy! who have no home on the earth or in the shades” whereas Carson’s says “I’m a strange new kind of inbetween thing aren’t I” about her dilemma.</p>

<p>Other projects of hers veer into forms the ancient world would have had trouble recognizing. She collaborated with artist <a href="https://www.rosannabruno.com/">Rosanna Bruno</a> on a <a href="https://www.ndbooks.com/book/the-trojan-women/">2021 graphic novel adaptation</a> of Euripides’ play “The Trojan Women,” first performed in 415 B.C.E. In 2025, she even <a href="https://rheostatics.ca/posts/2026-04-15-the-great-lakes-suite-for-sale-now/">read her poems on an album</a> for the indie rock band Rheostatics. Dave Bidini, one of the band’s founding members, <a href="https://www.cbc.ca/player/play/video/9.7373925">described Carson</a> as an artist who “hasn’t been afraid to experiment with language, to carve a place that’s her own with her work.”</p>

Anne Carson)" target="_blank">Thursday 12 pm Swimming (feat. Anne Carson)</a></div>

<h2>Leaving space for imagination</h2>

<p>The originality of her contribution can also arise from a refusal to do what many tend to expect from translations of ancient works in particular.</p>

<p>“<a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/160692/if-not-winter-by-sappho-translated-by-anne-carson/">If Not, Winter</a>,” her 2002 translation of Sappho, drew attention to the fragmentary nature of Sappho’s surviving work. </p>

<p><a href="https://access.infobase.com/article/1458872-sappho">Only one complete poem</a> of Sappho’s entire corpus exists: her “<a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/1621146/1-deathless-aphrodite">Ode to Aphrodite</a>.” Of the remaining fragments, some are lengthy, some only a word or two long, often quoted by other ancient authors. A number were found in shreds of papyri likely recycled to <a href="https://public.archive.wsu.edu/delahoyd/public_html/mythology/sappho.html">wrap mummies</a>.</p>

<p>In her translation, where papyri <a href="https://www.uni-koeln.de/phil-fak/ifa/NRWakademie/papyrologie/Verstreutepub/bilder/PK21351+21376r.jpg">were tattered</a> or a word <a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ostrakon_PSI_XIII_1300,_II_sec._ac,_frammento_di_un%27ode_di_saffo_sul_culto_di_afrodite.JPG">obscured</a>, Carson indicates this by <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/1621409/26-frequently-for-those">using brackets</a> and <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/1621141/24d-in-a-thin-voice">white space</a>. Rather than eliding them, Carson ends up bringing attention to these absences – an utterly distinctive choice. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Scan of papyri fragments with ancient Greek text" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=373&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=373&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=373&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=469&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=469&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765305/original/file-20261009-60-hh11rd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=469&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Much of Sappho’s surviving work exists only in fragments.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://digital.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/objects/92f6eaa7-4ba5-4c33-9888-7827f503e778/">Oxford, Bodleian Library MS. Gr. class. c. 76 (P)/1-2</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Carson states in the introduction to the translation that the brackets “imply a free space of imaginal adventure,” an invitation to fill in the blank of language now lost to us. Additionally, as <a href="https://www.emilyrcwilson.com/">classicist and translator Emily Wilson</a> notes, Carson “<a href="https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v26/n01/emily-wilson/tongue-breaks">adds no possessive pronouns or definite articles</a>” that are not present in the Greek, another way she lets contemporary readers meet Sappho’s fragments head on. </p>

<p>Where Carson lets an ancient voice speak without interposition, some have found “<a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2002/08/26/books/books-of-the-times-the-mystery-of-sappho-and-her-erotic-legacy.html">her particular kind of austerity</a>” wanting. Wilson, for instance, is critical of Carson’s refusal to tilt her translation in a way that acknowledges the important role that Sappho’s <a href="https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/acref/9780191834837.001.0001/acref-9780191834837-e-340">gender and sexuality</a> have played in her reception over time. </p>

<p>Wilson <a href="https://www.thenation.com/article/archive/violent-grace-anne-carsons-oresteia">further critiques</a> Carson’s “<a href="https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780865479166/anoresteia/">An Oresteia</a>,” her 2010 translation and adaptation of plays by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides. </p>

<p>Wilson writes that Carson “is acutely conscious of the differences, in mood, worldview and style, among the three tragedians she translates. It is, then, a disappointment that she does not entirely succeed in making them sound properly distinct from one another.”</p>

<h2>A running dialogue with literary greats</h2>

<p>It may be that the most distinctive voice in Carson’s translations of ancient authors is her own. But even her original work owes an evident debt to the words of others. She writes with and through other literary voices throughout her work.</p>

<p>Her long poem “<a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/48636/the-glass-essay">The Glass Essay</a>” explores romantic heartbreak and familial sorrow in dialogue with the life and work of Emily Brontë. </p>

<p>“<a href="https://www.ndbooks.com/book/nox/">Nox</a>,” an art book and work of poetry <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/books/book-picks/157991/-nox">created after her brother’s passing</a>, is also an exploration of the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2010/06/13/books/review/Ratliff-t.html">elegy that the Roman poet Catullus wrote to his own brother</a> over 2,000 years before. </p>

<p>And this is what Carson so often does so well: She draws the past into the present and refreshes it for us with a poet’s capacity for language and a classicist’s awareness of the long legacy of literature.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294020/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Why fall yard care could start with doing less – but not nothing</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765262/original/file-20261009-50-vzvluc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=446%2C0%2C4819%2C3213&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Leaves on the ground are part of the natural cycle of nutrients.</span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Manjot Sidhu</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Every autumn, homeowners and gardeners tend to engage in a familiar ritual. As trees shed their leaves, people drag out rakes, leaf blowers and lawn bags to strip their yards bare before winter arrives. </p>

<p>It is a tidy habit rooted in aesthetics, but ecologically, clearing away fallen leaves strips the very foundation of local ecosystems. Far from dead debris requiring disposal, this fallen foliage forms a dynamic layer and a biological interface that drives nutrient cycling and is <a href="https://extension.illinois.edu/blogs/garden-scoop/2017-11-08-fall-garden-cleanup-and-wildlife">essential for soil health and the environment, including biodiversity</a>.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=eQAsesUAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">researcher of plant growth</a> in yards and gardens, I would recommend leaving leaves on the ground. There, they can provide essential <a href="https://extension.psu.edu/programs/master-gardener/counties/lackawanna/news/how-to-support-our-pollinators-insects-and-birds-during-the-winter-months">winter habitat for native pollinators</a> – even in places that don’t have freezing temperatures. And they act as a <a href="https://www.lsuagcenter.com/articles/page1669123105183">nutrient-dense, natural mulch</a> for the soil. </p>

<p>Here is the science behind why the first step of fall yard care could simply be doing less – along with practical ways to keep your yard looking neat while nourishing the ecosystem underneath.</p>

<h2>A winter sanctuary for native pollinators</h2>

<p>To understand why leaf litter matters, it helps to look closely at what happens beneath the surface as temperatures drop. While honeybees pass the winter in <a href="https://environmentamerica.org/massachusetts/articles/what-do-bees-do-in-the-winter/">sheltered hives</a>, the vast majority of North America’s native pollinators do not. </p>

<p>Up to 70% of native bee species, including many insects’ cocoons and larvae, <a href="https://xerces.org/pollinator-conservation/nesting-resources">nest in the ground</a>. Fertilized queen bumblebees burrow <a href="https://xerces.org/pollinator-conservation/nesting-resources">just a few inches into the soil or hide under dense leaf mulch</a> to survive the freezing months ahead, to lay eggs in the following spring.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A bee flies among a group of flowers." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765057/original/file-20261008-50-t4y721.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">If bees and other pollinators are to return in the spring, they need somewhere to shelter in the winter.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/los-angeles-ca-birds-eye-gilia-is-seen-in-the-yard-of-news-photo/2177502429">Dania Maxwell/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Raking, bagging and blowing leaves away destroys this crucial winter nursery.</p>

<p>Many other insects depend on the shelter of fallen foliage:</p>

<ul>
<li><p>Moths and butterflies: Species such as the <a href="https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/47916-Actias-luna">luna moth (<em>Actias luna</em>)</a> and the Isabella tiger moth, whose <a href="https://www.keystone.edu/2026/10/07/woolly-bears-on-campus-folklore-fall-and-the-facts/">caterpillar form is the woolly bear</a>, spin cocoons or roll themselves directly inside fallen leaves. Raking or shredding those leaves destroys the next generation.</p></li>
<li><p>Fireflies: Adult fireflies lay eggs in moist soil, and their larvae spend up to two years hunting for their food, <a href="https://blog.nwf.org/2024/09/leave-the-leaves-to-save-fireflies/">soft-bodied invertebrates under damp leaf litter</a>. Raking deprives them of moisture and habitat.</p></li>
<li><p><a href="https://ipm.ucanr.edu/natural-enemies/predaceous-ground-beetles/#gsc.tab=0">Predatory ground beetles</a>: These beneficial predators <a href="https://www.lsuagcenter.com/%7E/media/system/b/8/4/b/b84bc30880b73ecdd797defdedd2cec7/p3949%20maintainingleaflitter_rh924pdf.pdf">spend the winter under leaves</a>, emerging in spring to feed on common garden pests such as aphids, slugs and mites. </p></li>
</ul>

<h2>Nature’s engineered soil insulator and fertilizer</h2>

<p>In addition to being a shelter, <a href="https://njaes.rutgers.edu/fs1369/">fallen leaves are an evolved biological mechanism for nutrient cycling</a>. Trees actively pump vital elements, including calcium, magnesium, potassium and nitrogen from deep subsoils, into their foliage. When autumn comes and leaves drop, these stored nutrients are deposited back into the soil.</p>

<p>Leaving leaves in place triggers fundamental ecological benefits.</p>

<p>A thick blanket of intact leaves acts as a natural insulator for the ground. Air pockets trapped between overlapping leaves moderate the soil temperature and slow heat transfer, <a href="https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/faq/what-frost-heaving-and-how-do-i-prevent-it">buffering against the freeze-thaw cycles that heave soil</a>, fracture plant roots and expose beneficial soil microbes to lethal cold. The intact leaf blanket also conserves moisture and prevents soil from drying out over the winter.</p>

<p>As fungi, earthworms and micro-arthropods digest fallen leaves through late fall and spring, they <a href="https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/humus/">break down organic matter into a rich material called humus</a>. This slow-release organic fertilizer boosts soil structure, improves water retention in sandy soils, and <a href="https://wcsoilworks.com/humus-versatile-and-close-to-nature/">prevents erosion and runoff in heavy rains</a>.</p>

<p>Decaying leaves feed beneficial mycorrhizal fungi in the soil. Those fungi form <a href="https://njaes.rutgers.edu/FS1384/">symbiotic relationships with plant and tree roots</a>, helping the roots collect water and nutrients from the soil to nourish the plants above. A natural layer of leaves also <a href="https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/using-leaves-in-the-landscape/">suppresses spring weed seeds</a> organically without needing synthetic chemical herbicides. And the moist, insulated microclimate under leaf litter is also critical for <a href="https://njaes.rutgers.edu/fs1369/">terrestrial amphibians, including frogs and salamanders</a>, to survive freezing temperatures.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Fallen leaves spread across a grassy area." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765059/original/file-20261008-70-iajxjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Leaves can also harbor ticks, but if you move them to places people don’t frequent, even in the warmer months, you can reduce the number of ticks in places with activity.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/arcadia-ca-colorful-oak-leaves-line-the-pathways-at-the-los-news-photo/2186864492=">David Crane/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>How to ‘leave the leaves’</h2>

<p>Adopting a softer approach to fall cleanup does not mean your yard has to look completely untamed or that you have to <a href="https://www.southernliving.com/hidden-dangers-leaves-lawn-12129619">risk killing your lawn</a>. Here is how to balance suburban expectations with sound ecological science:</p>

<ul>
<li><p>Move, don’t remove: Move the leaves from lawns and sidewalks, rake them into garden beds, around ornamental plants or into vegetable plots, using manual rakes or electric leaf blowers. Aim for a layer 2 to 3 inches deep. Leaving leaves in grassy areas can <a href="https://www.capecod.gov/2025/11/25/leave-the-leaves-cape-cod/">help ticks hide there too</a>, but if you move the leaves to garden beds or spots that are used less, the ticks will be less likely to nest in the grass. Establishing <a href="https://tickfreenh.org/reduce-ticks-while-supporting-pollinators-in-your-yard/">pollinator zones</a> on the property can also help reduce tick populations.</p></li>
<li><p>Skip the leaf shredder: Mowing over leaves with a mulching mower is better than sending them to landfills, but high-velocity mower blades still kill overwintering insect eggs, chrysalises and larvae. Leave leaves intact wherever possible in plant beds.</p></li>
<li><p>Wait for spring to clean up: Do not cut back hollow-stemmed perennials or clear leaf beds during early, warm spring days. Wait until temperatures consistently stay above 50 degrees Fahrenheit (10 degrees Celsius) so overwintering bees and butterflies <a href="https://engagement.source.colostate.edu/meant-to-bee-the-overwintering-strategies-of-bees-and-how-we-can-help/">have time to safely emerge</a>.</p></li>
</ul>

<p>When you bag leaves for disposal and then buy commercial wood mulch or synthetic fertilizers in the spring, you are effectively paying a price for what your trees provided for free. By rethinking the cultural expectation of pristine autumn lawns, it’s possible to transform silent landscapes into vibrant habitat sanctuaries, simply by stepping back and allowing natural processes to take over.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293924/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Leaves on the ground are part of the natural cycle of nutrients
Manjot Sidhu , CC BY-SA Every autumn, homeowners and gardeners tend to engage in a familiar ritual
As trees shed their leaves, people drag out rakes, leaf blowers and lawn bags to strip their yards bare before winter arrives
It is a tidy habit rooted in aesthetics, but ecologically, clearing away fallen leaves strips the very foundation of local ecosystems

Far from dead debris requiring disposal, this fallen foliage forms a dynamic layer and a biological interface that drives nutrient cycling and is essential for soil health and the environment, including biodiversity
As a researcher of plant growth in yards and gardens, I would recommend leaving leaves on the ground
There, they can provide essential winter habitat for native pollinators – even in places that don’t have freezing temperatures
And they act as a nutrient-dense, natural mulch for the soil
Here is the science behind why the first step of fall yard care could simply be doing less – along with practical ways to keep your yard looking neat while nourishing the ecosystem underneath
A winter sanctuary for native pollinators To understand why leaf litter matters, it helps to look closely at what happens beneath the surface as temperatures drop
While honeybees pass the winter in sheltered hives , the vast majority of North America’s native pollinators do not
Up to 70% of native bee species, including many insects’ cocoons and larvae, nest in the ground
Fertilized queen bumblebees burrow just a few inches into the soil or hide under dense leaf mulch to survive the freezing months ahead, to lay eggs in the following spring
If bees and other pollinators are to return in the spring, they need somewhere to shelter in the winter
Dania Maxwell/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Raking, bagging and blowing leaves away destroys this crucial winter nursery

Many other insects depend on the shelter of fallen foliage: Moths and butterflies: Species such as the luna moth ( Actias luna ) and the Isabella tiger moth, whose caterpillar form is the woolly bear , spin cocoons or roll themselves directly inside fallen leaves
Raking or shredding those leaves destroys the next generation
Fireflies: Adult fireflies lay eggs in moist soil, and their larvae spend up to two years hunting for their food, soft-bodied invertebrates under damp leaf litter
Raking deprives them of moisture and habitat
Predatory ground beetles : These beneficial predators spend the winter under leaves , emerging in spring to feed on common garden pests such as aphids, slugs and mites
Nature’s engineered soil insulator and fertilizer In addition to being a shelter, fallen leaves are an evolved biological mechanism for nutrient cycling
Trees actively pump vital elements, including calcium, magnesium, potassium and nitrogen from deep subsoils, into their foliage
When autumn comes and leaves drop, these stored nutrients are deposited back into the soil
Leaving leaves in place triggers fundamental ecological benefits
A thick blanket of intact leaves acts as a natural insulator for the ground

Air pockets trapped between overlapping leaves moderate the soil temperature and slow heat transfer, buffering against the freeze-thaw cycles that heave soil , fracture plant roots and expose beneficial soil microbes to lethal cold
The intact leaf blanket also conserves moisture and prevents soil from drying out over the winter
As fungi, earthworms and micro-arthropods digest fallen leaves through late fall and spring, they break down organic matter into a rich material called humus
This slow-release organic fertilizer boosts soil structure, improves water retention in sandy soils, and prevents erosion and runoff in heavy rains
Decaying leaves feed beneficial mycorrhizal fungi in the soil
Those fungi form symbiotic relationships with plant and tree roots , helping the roots collect water and nutrients from the soil to nourish the plants above
A natural layer of leaves also suppresses spring weed seeds organically without needing synthetic chemical herbicides
And the moist, insulated microclimate under leaf litter is also critical for terrestrial amphibians, including frogs and salamanders , to survive freezing temperatures
Leaves can also harbor ticks, but if you move them to places people don’t frequent, even in the warmer months, you can reduce the number of ticks in places with activity

David Crane/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images How to ‘leave the leaves’ Adopting a softer approach to fall cleanup does not mean your yard has to look completely untamed or that you have to risk killing your lawn

Here is how to balance suburban expectations with sound ecological science: Move, don’t remove: Move the leaves from lawns and sidewalks, rake them into garden beds, around ornamental plants or into vegetable plots, using manual rakes or electric leaf blowers
Leaving leaves in grassy areas can help ticks hide there too , but if you move the leaves to garden beds or spots that are used less, the ticks will be less likely to nest in the grass
Establishing pollinator zones on the property can also help reduce tick populations
Skip the leaf shredder: Mowing over leaves with a mulching mower is better than sending them to landfills, but high-velocity mower blades still kill overwintering insect eggs, chrysalises and larvae
Leave leaves intact wherever possible in plant beds
